title: Drive a cap screw into a threaded insert with a screwdriver, holding the screw, then the screwdriver, upright
instruction: Screw the steel cap screw into the brass insert with the red screwdriver. Pick up the screw and the screwdriver from where they lie, stand the screw up in the insert's mouth and hold it there, put the screwdriver's hex bit into the screw's socket, then turn the screwdriver clockwise, seen from above, until the screw's head sits on top of the insert. Neither the screw nor the screwdriver stays standing on its own until the screw is driven in, so keep one of them held while the other hand works.
context: Driving a screw with a hand screwdriver is one of the most common steps in assembly and repair. Here nothing is started or held for the robot: both parts lie loose, the screw stands in its hole only while held until the bit is in its socket, and each time the turning hand lets go to regrip, the other hand has to be holding the screwdriver up.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A brass threaded insert, a cylinder 1.7 cm across and 2.5 cm tall, fixed upright to the table at 30 cm forward, 16 cm right; its bore has a right-hand thread 12 mm across with a 3 mm pitch and a 1.5 mm chamfer at its mouth. (2) A steel socket cap screw (20 g) with a dark oxide head: a round knurled head 2 cm across and 1.2 cm tall with a 10 mm hex socket 6 mm deep (its mouth countersunk 2.5 mm), on a 9 mm threaded shank matching the insert. It lies on its side on the table, its head's centre at 22 cm forward, 12 cm left, its tip pointing back toward the left arm's base. (3) A screwdriver (80 g, 16 cm long): a red rubber octagonal handle 2.6 cm across the flats and 6 cm long, on a 9 mm round steel shaft ending in a 9.6 mm hex bit 1.2 cm long with a tapered tip. It lies on a flat of its handle, the handle's centre at 24 cm forward, 30 cm right, its bit pointing back toward the right arm's base. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, from the screw's and the screwdriver's poses. Gap: the height of the screw head's underside above the insert's top. The screw is standing in the insert when the gap is under 9 mm (its tip inside the insert), its axis is within 10 degrees of vertical and the centre of the head's underside is within 2 mm of the insert's axis. The bit is in the socket when its tip is at least 2 mm below the socket's top, within 1.5 mm of the screw's axis, with the two axes within 10 degrees. Score: 0.0 unless the screw is standing in the insert; 0.2 if it is but the bit is not in its socket, however far the screw is in (a screw turned in by its head, not with the screwdriver, scores no more); with the bit in the socket, 0.3 plus 0.7 times the share of the way driven, from a gap of 7.0 mm (the screw set in the insert's mouth) to 0.6 mm (seated). 1.0: seated, with a gap under 0.6 mm, the axis within 3 degrees of vertical and within 1 mm of the insert's axis, and the bit in the socket, held for 1 s; the trial then ends, otherwise it ends at the run limit.
reset_notes: Unscrew the screw and lay it and the screwdriver back where they started.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). The threads are real helical surfaces collided as signed distance fields: the screw advances only as it turns, about 2.9 mm per turn of its 3 mm pitch. Simplified: the pitch is coarser than a real M12's (1.75 mm), so seating takes about 2.3 turns; thread friction 0.3; a screw left in the thread creeps about 0.25 degrees a second; the insert is fixed. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
